The reason this is urgent rather than tidy: ships switch their transponders OFF more often exactly when a war zone gets worse, so the tracker shows a drop in barrels when nothing has actually stopped flowing. name: Credit gate: which way of measuring bad loans should count?
what: BROCK's BRK-02 gate watches how much of six private-credit funds' loans have stopped paying. There are two standard ways to measure that, and they currently point in OPPOSITE directions. In OBDC's own quarterly filing, bad loans ROSE 2.3% -> 2.8% measured at original cost, and FELL 1.1% -> 0.8% measured at current market value, over the same two quarters. The written narrative in that filing quotes the falling number; the table behind it shows the rising one. BRK-02's rule never says which to use.
why_yours: It changes the gate's answer, and only you rule what a gate reads. Measured at cost, two of the six funds are already above the 2.5% line; measured at market value, the picture looks benign. Same funds, same quarter, opposite readings.
if_yes: Pick amortized cost and the letter says so plainly: the gate reads two of six above the line today, and it stops depending on which paragraph of a filing you happen to read.
if_no: Pick fair value and the gate stays quiet -- but understand why it stays quiet, which is the next box.
if_nothing: The gate keeps an unnamed basis, and whoever grades it next picks one without knowing they picked.
rec_reason: Rec: amortized cost. The reason is mechanical, not a preference: when a loan is written down, its own value shrinks, so it counts for less in the very measure that is supposed to flag it -- one OBDC name fell from $135.3M to $8.3M. A fair-value basis therefore looks BETTER as credit gets WORSE. That is a gate that goes quiet exactly when it should fire. BROCK found this, flagged it, and deliberately did NOT resolve it because it judged itself conflicted -- which is why it is your call and not an encoded change.
